name: Alginate filler

lead: Alginate is a polysaccharide extracted from brown seaweed that forms a gel when linked with calcium. It is listed among the natural polymers used or explored for injectable dermal fillers.
The appeal for appearance is the same as other fillers: a soft gel placed under the skin adds volume to areas such as cheeks, lips or folds.

paras: Fillers are placed by a trained injector into targeted facial areas. Hyaluronic acid products dominate clinical use; alginate-based gels are more often described in materials research.
Fillers in general carry bruising, swelling, infection and allergic reaction risks, and rare vascular complications. Specific safety data on alginate fillers are limited.

angle.text: As with other fillers, an injected gel adds soft-tissue volume to reshape contours.

lead: Alginate filler refers to the use of alginate, a hydrophilic polysaccharide from brown algae, as an injectable gel material for adding volume to the face.[1][2]

Alginate forms a hydrogel when calcium cross-links it under mild aqueous conditions. It is already used in wound dressings, dental impressions and as a cosmetic thickener.[1] Dermal filler overviews list alginate among naturally derived polymers alongside gelatin, collagen and chitosan, though hyaluronic acid is the most common filler.[2]
Typical wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting around six months, and carry risks that range from bruising to rare vascular events.[2]

paras: Alginic acid comes from brown seaweeds such as giant kelp and forms viscous gels; with calcium it becomes a cross-linked hydrogel.[1] Its other uses include Gaviscon and drug-delivery research.[1]
Filler complications in general include bruising, redness, infection, allergic reactions and, rarely, blindness from vessel embolisation or skin necrosis.[2]
